newsitem.title: USA: NYS gov says wants to "bridge" clash on rent rules.
newsitem.headline: NYS gov says wants to "bridge" clash on rent rules.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki on Tuesday said he would try to "bridge" the clash between Democratic and Republican lawmakers over rent rules, but declined to be drawn about some of his own views.

"I don't want to do as a great many others are which is politically posture, and put out political statements, I want to solve the problem and bridge the gap between the Senate and the Assembly, and beyond that I'm not going to comment any more on specifics of rent control," Pataki told reporters in Albany.

New York City Council Peter Vallone, who is running for re-election but is seen as a potential Democratic governor for governor in 1998, called upon Pataki to show some leadership over the issue, which is especially important for New York City, as it has most of the state's rent-regulated apartments.

"Let's cut out the games. They're not fair to either landlords or tenants," said Vallone in a prepared statement. He cited reports of a landlord who wrote a tenant that he planned to raise his rent by about 337 percent because he understood rent regulations would expire on June 15.

Pataki dismissed Vallone's remarks as typical for someone who might be running for higher office, but noted he also wanted to end the gamesmenship "It's obviously just political from someone who has indicated that he may be a candidate for higher office."

The Republican governor's remarks in turn brought a sharp response from Vallone. "The governor cannot brush the rent cotnrol issue aside. The fact is the ball's in his court and he needs to act," Vallone added, in a statement released by his spokeswoman.

Pataki, who previously has signaled his support for some ways of ending rent rules, like vacancy decontrol, made it plain that he might favor further limiting rules that aim to stop well-to-do individuals from taking advantage of rent regulations.

"Obviously, we want to protect the existing tenants, who deserve protection. I don't think someone who makes $250,000 a year and has a million dollar estate upstate necessarily should be covered by rent control laws."

He added that both the Democrat-led Assembly, which wants the present rules permanently extended, and the Republican-controlled Senate, which has threatened to let them expire on June 15, both will have to compromise.

Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, wants a new bill approved that protects needy, eldery and disabled tenants while ending protections for others, over a two-year or perhaps a four-year timeframe.

Another key figure in the battle over rent rules, which is one of the main issues holding up the state's budget that was due on April 1, is U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican who carries considerable weight in local matters. He was quoted by the New York Times on Tuesday as saying a 10-year phase-out of rent rules would be too quick. "That's still too sudden," he told the paper. "It would still blow things up."
Pataki, who closely coordinates his actions with the Republican Senator, said he did not want to get into specifics when asked about D'Amato's comments.
